opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the really interesting open questions, and it's a place where I think robotics is going to force us to come up with some new ideas rather than just borrowing everything from language models.

The basic issue is that a robot is getting this firehose of data. You've got multiple cameras running at, say, 30 or 50 hertz, proprioception, maybe touch sensing, and if you naively tokenize all of that and stuff it into a transformer's context, you run out of room after a few seconds. But the tasks we actually care about, like cleaning up a kitchen or folding laundry, play out over minutes or hours. So there's a big mismatch between how much raw data comes in and how much the model can actually reason over.

I think there are a few places where algorithms can help. The first is just recognizing that most of that stream is extremely redundant. If I'm looking at a table and nothing is moving, the next frame tells me almost nothing new. People are actually pretty good at this. You don't remember every photon that hit your retina over the last ten minutes. You remember something like "I put the cup over there, the drawer is open, I still need to wipe the counter." So one big opportunity is learning representations that compress the past into something much more abstract and task-relevant, rather than keeping it all around in raw form.

The second is the separation of time scales. The low-level motor control has to be fast. You need to react within tens of milliseconds if something slips. But the higher-level reasoning, figuring out what to do next or whether a subtask worked, can be much slower and more deliberate. So you can imagine architectures where a fast system works with a very short, high-resolution window of recent observations, and a slower system works with a long, heavily compressed history. That's somewhat analogous to how we've been thinking about combining vision-language models with action experts, where different parts of the model operate at different granularities.

The third, and maybe the most interesting one to me, is that the right compression is something the model should learn from the task itself, not something we hand-design. It's tempting to say "let's just keep keyframes" or "let's do some fixed downsampling," and those heuristics help. But what actually matters depends on what you're trying to do. If you're searching for your keys, the moment you glanced at the counter matters a lot. If you're folding a shirt, it doesn't. So I think the long-term answer looks like models that learn what to remember and what to throw away, probably trained with some combination of large-scale prediction objectives and reinforcement learning, so the memory gets shaped by whether it's actually useful for succeeding at the task.

And I'd add one more thing: there's a nice synergy here with how language models do reasoning. A robot can sort of narrate to itself, summarizing in text or in some latent form what's happened so far and what comes next. That's a very compact form of memory. It's not the whole answer, because lots of physical knowledge isn't easily put into words, but it's a pretty powerful tool, and we're just starting to figure out how to use it well.

r001.rationale: The response says consecutive observations are often redundant and recommends compressing the history instead of retaining raw observations, clearly conveying that temporal correlations enable compression.

r002.rationale: The response discusses possible learned memory and compression approaches, but does not say implementation should wait until the machine-learning solution’s form is known.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more interesting questions in robotics right now, because the naive answer is kind of unsatisfying. The naive answer is: you have a camera streaming at 30 frames a second, you have proprioception coming in at hundreds of hertz, maybe tactile sensors on top of that, and you just push all of it through a big network and hope it figures out what matters. And to some degree that works. But it's wasteful in a way that I think points at where the algorithmic opportunities are.

The first thing to notice is that the sensory stream is enormously redundant. If you're looking at a kitchen counter and reaching for a mug, most of what the camera sees frame to frame is identical. The world didn't change. Your arm moved a little. So there's a sense in which the information content of the stream is much lower than the raw bit rate, and a good representation should exploit that. Humans obviously do this. You don't re-perceive the whole scene every 33 milliseconds, you maintain some belief about the world and update it where something surprised you.

So one opportunity is in learned representations that are explicitly predictive. If you train a model to predict what the next observation will be given your action, then the thing you actually need to attend to is the residual, the part you couldn't predict. That's where the new information is. And that reframing is nice because it turns a computational problem into a learning problem. You're not hand-designing which pixels to drop, you're learning what's predictable and therefore safe to compress.

The second opportunity, which I think is more underexplored, is about temporal abstraction. Right now most policies operate at a fixed control frequency, and we treat that as kind of a given. But there's no reason the frequency of decision-making has to match the frequency of sensing. A lot of what the robot is doing is executing something it already committed to. When you reach for the mug, you decided to reach for the mug, and then the next half second is mostly closed-loop refinement that doesn't need the full perceptual stack. So you can imagine architectures where a slow, expensive, high-level process looks at the scene occasionally and sets intent, and a fast, cheap, low-level process handles the moment-to-moment stuff using a much smaller sensory footprint. We've seen hints of this working with action chunking, where the policy outputs a sequence of actions rather than one, and it turns out that's often better, not just cheaper, probably because it's smoothing over noise in the perception.

And then the third thing I'd point at is the role of memory and state. If you have a good internal state estimate, you can afford to be selective about what you look at. The classic version of this is active perception, where the robot moves its camera or its attention to where the information is. But even without physically moving anything, you can have a model that decides which part of the image to process at high resolution and which to skip. Foveation, essentially. Transformers make this fairly natural because attention is already a selection mechanism, so the question becomes whether you can make that selection sparse enough to actually save compute rather than just reweight everything.

I'll be honest that there's a tension here. The bitter-lesson view says don't be clever, just scale, the model will learn to ignore what doesn't matter. And there's real truth to that. But robots have a constraint that language models don't, which is that they have to act in real time on hardware that's often sitting on the robot itself. You can't batch your way out of latency. So I think this is one of the places where algorithmic ideas about what to attend to and when actually matter, not because scaling doesn't work, but because the physical world imposes a budget that forces you to be smart about where you spend it.

r001.rationale: The response says consecutive observations are highly redundant and proposes predicting the next observation, then focusing on the unpredictable residual as a way to compress the stream.

r002.rationale: The response frames some computational choices as learning problems, but does not argue that implementation should wait until the machine-learning solution’s form is known.

astra-6.text:
I think a big opportunity is deciding what deserves computation. A robot gets this continuous stream of images and other sensory inputs, but much of it is redundant. If you’re sitting in a room and nothing is changing, you probably don’t need to process every frame with the same amount of effort. But if something unexpected happens—an object starts slipping out of your hand—you need to react very quickly.

So you’d like a system that maintains some internal understanding of what’s going on, predicts what it expects to see, and spends more computation when the observations depart from that prediction. The tricky part is that relevance depends on what you’re doing. A small change in an image might be irrelevant when you’re navigating across a room and critical when you’re threading a needle.

There’s also an opportunity to reason at different timescales. You don’t need to reconsider your entire plan every time you issue a motor command. You could make a higher-level decision relatively infrequently, while a much cheaper controller handles the details. Learning those representations and those timescales, so that you preserve the information that matters for acting, seems like a very promising direction.

r001.rationale: The response notes redundancy and prediction in sensory streams, but does not say temporal correlations enable greater compression than representing observations independently.

r002.rationale: The response discusses learning representations and timescales, but does not say implementation should wait until the machine-learning solution is known.

sol-6.1.text:
One opportunity is to recognize that a robot doesn’t need to process every bit of sensory input with the same amount of computation. If you’re reaching for a cup, you need fairly precise information about where the cup is and how your hand is moving relative to it. You probably don’t need to continually reconsider everything in the background.

So you could have a system that maintains a representation of what’s going on and updates it selectively. Some computations might run very quickly, like the feedback loop controlling your hand. Other computations, like deciding what you’re going to do next, can run much more slowly. And an unexpected event could trigger more computation: if the cup slips, now you need to pay attention and revise what you’re doing.

The interesting algorithmic question is how much of that structure we can learn. Can the robot learn what information to retain, what to ignore, and when to invoke a more expensive computation? Ideally, you’d learn representations that preserve the information you need for making decisions, without having to reconstruct every detail of the sensory stream. That could make long-running, continuous interaction much more tractable.

r001.rationale: It describes selective updates and retaining useful information, but does not state that temporal correlations enable greater compression than independently representing each observation.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning what to retain and when to compute, but does not say implementation should wait until the machine-learning solution’s form is known.
